I've been farming these 8 mu in Quzhou for over forty years. My father did the same before me. At 62, I don't have the energy or the cash to gamble on fancy new crops, so I'll stick with what I know: winter wheat followed by summer maize. That's what the whole village does, and it feeds my family.

For the wheat, I'll sow in mid-October after rotary tilling the field. I'll use the improved Jinmai variety I've saved seed from for two years now — it's reliable and I don't have to pay for new bags every year. I'll put down about 18 kg of nitrogen per mu total: half as compound fertilizer at planting, half as urea topdress when the wheat greens up and at jointing. The extension agent keeps saying 15 kg is enough, but two years ago I tried 15 and the plants looked yellow, so I went back to 18. I'll also put down some phosphorus and potassium with the basal dressing — about 5 kg each per mu. I can't afford soil tests, but I've learned that if I skip the P and K, the wheat gets weak-stemmed. I'll irrigate four times: once before winter to help it survive the cold, once at green-up in March, once at jointing, and once at grain filling. The pump electricity is expensive, but dry wheat means no bread. For sprays, I'll do three applications: a herbicide right after sowing, an insecticide in spring when the aphids come, and a fungicide at heading to keep rust away.

For the maize, I'll plant hybrid seed immediately after wheat harvest in early June — there's no time to plough, so I'll use no-tillage direct seeding. I always buy fresh hybrid seed because saved maize seed loses vigor. I'll apply 15 kg of nitrogen per mu, mostly as a compound dressing at planting and one urea topdress at the big-flush stage. About 4 kg each of phosphorus and potassium per mu should be enough since the wheat already took a lot out. Maize doesn't need as much water as wheat if the summer rains cooperate, but I'll irrigate twice — at jointing and at filling — just to be safe. Two pesticide sprays: a herbicide at emergence and one insecticide for corn borers in July.

I expect about 500 kg per mu from the wheat and 550 kg per mu from the maize. If the weather is good and the market price doesn't collapse, that should cover my input costs and leave enough for my grandson's school fees.
